title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica.
authors: Schuster, Layla A; Liu, Beibei; Silva, Jose Cleydson F; Cheng, Xi; Dias, Raquel; Zhao, Meixia
abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility.
authors: Lee, Jodi; Zhang, Kaite; Shurberg, Ethan; Ramani, Vijay; Pollard, Katherine S
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis -regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

title: A high-resolution protein-RNA binding atlas for structure-aware interaction prediction and post-transcriptional regulatory modeling.
authors: Karimzadeh, Mehran; Fish, Lisa; Karner, Heather; Linder, Johannes; Emadi, Ali; Hernandez-Corchado, Aldo; Smaili, Fatima Zohra; Ghavami, Khashayar; Stewart, Edna S; Kelley, David; Wang, Bo; Najafabadi, Hamed Shateri; Leonetti, Manuel D; Goodarzi, Hani
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) control post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating RNA processing, localization, stability, and translation. However, our understanding of RNA regulation remains limited by the resolution, scale, and uniformity of available RBP binding maps. Here we introduce eclair CLIP (ecCLIP), a high-throughput CLIP-seq platform that combines endogenous protein tagging for uniform affinity capture with ligation-free library preparation to generate high-resolution RNA-protein binding profiles. We applied ecCLIP to 67 endogenously tagged RBPs in HEK293T cells, generating a high-quality transcriptome-scale atlas that recovered known binding preferences and captured post-transcriptional regulons linked to RNA half-life. To test the utility of the atlas, we incorporated ecCLIP into Borzuki, a Borzoi-derived sequence-to-function model trained on complementary RNA degradation, expression, CLIP, and Perturb-seq data. Inclusion of ecCLIP data improved RNA half-life prediction and assessment of 3 (') UTR variant effects on RNA stability, demonstrating that our atlas helps capture RNA dynamics. To directly model the cis-regulatory grammar underlying these RBP-RNA interactions, we developed Pythia, a structure-aware neural network architecture that incorporates context-free grammar-inspired fixed convolutions to explicitly encode RNA base-pairing features. Pythia predicted RBP binding from sequence and structural context and decomposed predictions into sequence- and structure-dependent components. We tested this decomposition for five RBPs using massively parallel reporter CLIP (MPRC) binding assays in cells, using synthetic RNA libraries containing mutations designed to preserve or disrupt predicted RNA structures across nominated binding sites. We used the same MPRC strategy to confirm allele-specific binding effects for variants prioritized by Pythia. Together, ecCLIP and Pythia provide a resource for structure-aware decoding of RNA-protein interaction grammar and interpretation of post-transcriptional regulatory variation.

title: MultiFlow: coupled flow matching for predicting single-cell multiomic perturbation responses in unseen cellular contexts.
authors: Wang, Haochen; Zhang, Charming; Zhang, Mengran; Nie, Xiaoming; Liu, Qiao
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbation requires resolving coordinated changes across molecular layers, yet most single-cell perturbation models focus on transcriptional responses alone. Here we present MultiFlow, a coupled flow-matching framework that unifies generation and perturbation prediction of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Through bidirectional information exchange between RNA and ATAC generative flows, MultiFlow learns how their joint distribution depends on cellular context and perturbation identity. Across multiomic generation benchmarks, MultiFlow accurately reproduced paired RNA-ATAC states and their population distributions. In multiome perturbation benchmarks, MultiFlow achieved the strongest overall performance in predicting both gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility perturbation responses, outperforming modality-specific perturbation-prediction methods in cell types whose perturbed states were withheld from training. Joint multiomic modeling further preserved perturbation-induced coordination between modalities, including concordant peak-gene effects and cross-modal cellular neighborhood structure. These results establish MultiFlow as a unified generative framework for modeling paired molecular states and predicting their coordinated perturbation responses across cellular contexts. Code and tutorial of MultiFlow are available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.

title: Kidzoi Enables Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory Activity and Variant Effect Prediction in Kidney.
authors: Rather, Arif A; Lee, Dongwon
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) deep learning models predict genome-wide functional profiles directly from DNA sequences and have significantly advanced our understanding of gene regulation. However, existing S2F models are fundamentally constrained by their initial training datasets, and no single model encompasses the full spectrum of cell types, clinical conditions, and cellular states, while training new models de novo is nontrivial. Here, we develop Kidzoi, a kidney cell-type-specific S2F model obtained by transfer learning from the pretrained model Borzoi using single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from human kidney tissue. Kidzoi accurately predicts cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and improves regulatory variant effect prediction in proximal tubule cells by up to 23% in terms of AUROC over existing models. Furthermore, Kidzoi effectively prioritizes genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapped causal variants associated with kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate based on both creatinine and cystatin C; eGFRcr-cys) while resolving their cell-type specificity. Systematic ablation of flanking sequence indicates that a local context of 32-64 kbp , representing only 6-12% of the full model input, captures most of the information needed for variant effect prediction. Finally, we show that a multi-task model achieves comparable performance to single-task models at a substantially reduced computational cost.

title: MutFormer: a multimodal deep learning framework for predicting somatic mutation hotspots from sequence and chromatin features.
authors: Li, Tianbao; Jiang, Yan; Wu, Junjie; Lin, Junru; Widjaja, Reisa; Wang, Ailan; Liu, Qi; Zhou, Hongbo
abstract: BACKGROUND: Somatic mutations are unevenly distributed across the genome, with certain loci recurrently mutated across independent tumors. Both local DNA sequence context and chromatin organization have been associated with mutation rate variation, yet their combined effects at single-nucleotide resolution remain incompletely characterized. RESULTS: We developed MutFormer, a multimodal framework that integrates sequence context with chromatin-associated features to estimate mutation hotspot susceptibility at single-base resolution. Model performance was evaluated using a chromosome-partitioned strategy to reduce potential bias from local sequence similarity. The model achieved an AUROC of 0.979 and an AUPRC of 0.955 on TCGA data, and showed consistent performance on an independent METABRIC cohort. In addition to overall predictive accuracy, the integration of chromatin features altered the relative ranking of genomic loci. A subset of hotspot positions showed increased predicted susceptibility compared with sequence-only models, suggesting that chromatin context contributes information not captured by sequence composition alone. Sequence-derived features, particularly CpG-related metrics, accounted for the majority of predictive signal, whereas chromatin features provided a secondary, context-dependent contribution. The absolute AUROC gain from chromatin integration over the sequence-only model was modest (DeltaAUROC = 0.004). Chromatin features instead reordered the prediction ranks of a specific subset ( approximately 14%) of hotspot loci, with most loci unaffected. CONCLUSIONS: These results support a model in which intrinsic sequence composition defines baseline mutation susceptibility, while chromatin context modulates the relative prioritization of specific loci. This framework provides a complementary approach for identifying mutation-prone regions beyond sequence-based models. MutFormer runs in a sequence-only mode by default and incorporates chromatin features as an optional enhancement when matched data are available.

title: Truncating Kabuki Syndrome-associated KMT2D Mutation in FYR Domain Alters Chromatin Accessibility at Neurodevelopmental Loci.
authors: Ozden-Yilmaz, Gulden; Olmez, Akgun; Yilmazbilek, Irem; Tulu, Ahmet Can; Binokay, Leman; Gencpinar, Pinar; Hiz, Ayse Semra; Oktay, Yavuz; Karakulah, Gokhan; Karaca, Ezgi; Senturk, Serif; Erkek-Ozhan, Serap
abstract: Kabuki syndrome (KS) is a congenital neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, developmental delay, and multisystem involvement. KS is primarily caused by de novo mutations in KMT2D, a H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferase within the MLL3/4 COMPASS-like complex. Although the role of KMT2D in active chromatin organization is well established, the function of its FYR domain remains largely unknown. Here, we report a KS patient carrying a heterozygous KMT2D p.R5282* nonsense mutation located at the C-terminal side of the FYR domain. The patient exhibited a relatively mild phenotype, consistent with previously reported p.R5282* mutation carriers. ATAC-seq analysis of patient-derived PBMCs revealed 451 differentially accessible regions compared to controls, with reduced accessibility mainly at promoter regions of genes involved in neurogenesis. Motif and regulatory enrichment analyses identified loss of CTCF and WRAD complex components (WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L), suggesting impaired chromatin organization. To examine the functional impact of FYR mutations, we expressed FLAG-tagged KMT2D p.R5282* and another FYR domain hotspot missense mutation (p.R5179C) in HEK293T cells and performed ATAC-seq. p.R5282*-specific chromatin changes mirrored those in the patient and were enriched for promoter regions and WRAD binding sites, whereas p.R5179C showed distinct patterns. AlphaFold3 modeling indicated that p.R5282* truncation disrupts the WIN motif required for WDR5 binding, compromising MLL3/4 complex stability. Both the patient and p.R5282*-expressing cells showed reduced chromatin accessibility at the CHD7 locus, linking KMT2D dysfunction to CHARGE syndrome pathways. These findings highlight the essential role of the KMT2D FYR domain in maintaining WRAD complex integrity and chromatin accessibility.

title: Identification and expression analysis of intergenic long non-coding RNAs (lincRNA) associated with stripe rust resistance in wheat.
authors: Fang, Xiaole; Wang, Xiaoyu; Yang, Tian; Wang, Youning; Ao, Xue; Cao, Peina; Gong, Pan; Ma, Dongfang
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Long intergenic non-coding RNAs (lincRNAs) have emerged as important regulators of plant immune responses, yet their functional landscape in wheat (Triticum aestivum) during stripe rust (Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici) infection remains largely unexplored. METHODS: In this study, a genome-wide identification of lincRNAs was performed using strand-specific RNA-seq data from wheat leaves following Pst inoculation. Functional enrichment, co-expression, lincRNA-miRNA-mRNA network prediction, and AlphaFold-based protein-RNA structure prediction were used to characterize candidate lincRNAs. RESULTS: A total of 2,736 expressed lincRNAs were identified, of which 515 were differentially expressed during infection. Functional enrichment of genes located within 100 kb of the differentially expressed lincRNAs revealed significant associations with defense-related pathways, including MAPK signaling and plant-pathogen interaction. Coordinated expression patterns between lincRNAs and adjacent defense-related mRNAs suggested putative cis-regulatory associations. Furthermore, lincRNA-miRNA-mRNA network prediction identified 65 differentially expressed lincRNAs as potential endogenous target mimics for 21 conserved miRNAs, revealing a widespread competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) regulatory network. Importantly, AlphaFold-based protein-RNA structure prediction demonstrated that the co-expressed lincRNA MSTRG.56980 forms a stable complex with the RGA1-type resistance protein TraesCS6B03G0179100. DISCUSSION: This provides a first computational prediction of a possible physical interaction between a wheat lincRNA and an immune receptor. These integrative findings substantially expand the current understanding of non-coding regulatory networks in wheat immunity and provide a foundational resource for prioritizing candidate lincRNAs as targets for enhancing stripe rust resistance.

title: Polyphosphate and Disordered Hfq Regions Drive DNA Compaction through Conformation-Dependent Interactions.
authors: Navon, Yoav; Levy, Yaakov
abstract: The RNA-binding protein Hfq and inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) were previously suggested to promote DNA compaction of AT-rich regions by forming heterochromatin-like structures, yet the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the interplay between Hfq, polyP, and DNA. Under physiological conditions, polyP electrostatically interacts with the distal faces of multiple Hfq hexamers, clustering them near DNA and leaving the proximal faces available to interact with the DNA minor groove via the disordered N-termini, thereby promoting compaction. While this mechanism shows limited dependence on DNA sequence, it is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. Under high-salt conditions, electrostatic interactions are screened, weakening polyP-Hfq association and limiting Hfq clustering, while stabilization of non-canonical DNA conformations exposes hydrophobic surfaces. These changes shift the mode of Hfq interaction with DNA toward its distal face and disordered C-termini, favoring hydrophobic interactions and reducing compaction. Together, our findings reveal a conformation-dependent switch in Hfq-DNA interaction modes governed by cellular conditions, providing a molecular framework for environment-responsive genome organization in bacteria.

title: Deciphering the regulatory code of RNA inosine through enzymatic precision mapping and an explainable deep learning model.
authors: Han, Shaoqing; Li, Jiehua; Yang, Wei; Wei, Qi; Wang, Yafen; Zhou, Xiang; Weng, Xiaocheng
abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is one of the most abundant RNA modifications and is involved in multiple critical biological processes; however, the precise localization of inosine and the mechanisms governing their selective editing remain incompletely understood. Integrating high-accuracy detection technologies with deep learning models can accelerate our understanding of the selective positioning and functional implications of A-to-I editing. To address these challenges, this study simultaneously developed RNA inosine sequencing by endonuclease V (EndoV) and XRN-1 (REX-seq), a highly sensitive and accurate detection method for inosine sites, and Inosine Deep Residual Enhanced Attention Model (InoDREAM), a predictive deep learning framework. REX-seq combines EndoV cleavage specificity with XRN-1 exonuclease activity to enable comprehensive A-to-I editome profiling while maintaining accurate gene expression quantification. Using this method, we identified 590,249 high-confidence inosine sites in HEK293T cells, including 84,645 novel sites. Leveraging the high-confidence A-to-I editing sites identified by REX-seq, we developed InoDREAM, which successfully predicted multiple regulatory proteins that exhibit specific binding affinity to A-to-I edited transcripts while simultaneously identifying disease-associated mutation sites and relevant cis-regulatory elements that are functionally linked to RNA editing events. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights into both the molecular regulation of RNA editing and its pathophysiological implications in disease development.

title: Cancer-associated histone tail mutations reshape conformational ensembles and DNA-contact states in nucleosomes.
authors: Wang, Liujin; Zhang, Houfang; Yuan, Xupeng; Mai, Meiru; Zhao, Yunjie; Peng, Yunhui
abstract: Cancer-associated histone mutations can perturb chromatin regulation, yet how many noncanonical mutations in intrinsically disordered histone tails alter nucleosome dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we combine pan-cancer histone mutation profiling with 31.5 mus of all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of complete nucleosomes to investigate recurrent mutations in the H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 tails. We identify recurrent and understudied mutation sites beyond canonical H3 oncohistones and characterize how selected substitutions perturb histone-tail conformational ensembles and DNA contacts in their nucleosomal context. The simulations reveal mutation-specific redistribution of tail-DNA contacts across the nucleosomal DNA surface, accompanied by changes in MM/GBSA-derived relative interaction-energy estimates. For selected systems, Markov state modeling further resolves metastable tail-DNA contact states and shows that mutations alter their structural characteristics and population distributions. These perturbations are not confined to the substituted residues but extend to neighboring interaction networks. Together, our results provide a molecular-level physical picture of how cancer-associated histone-tail mutations reshape conformational and interaction-state landscapes in nucleosomes.

title: Nutrigenomics in Dairy Cattle: Causes and Implications.
authors: Tamasgen, Negasa; Asefa, Bacha
abstract: Nutrigenomics is a rapidly developing interdisciplinary field that investigates the interactions between nutrients and the genome, with particular emphasis on how dietary components regulate gene expression and metabolic pathways. In dairy cattle, nutrigenomics has gained increasing attention due to its potential to improve milk production, metabolic efficiency, health, reproduction, and overall animal performance. Nutrients and bioactive dietary compounds can influence gene activity directly through transcriptional regulation or indirectly through epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modification, and noncoding RNA-mediated gene regulation. These nutrigenomic interactions affect important biological processes including lipid metabolism, adipogenesis, immune response, mammary gland development, and milk synthesis. Advances in omics technologies including transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and next-generation sequencing have enhanced understanding of the molecular responses of dairy cows to nutritional interventions. Dietary fatty acids, vitamins, methyl donors, and short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate have been shown to regulate key transcription factors including peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), sterol regulatory element binding proteins (SREBPs), and liver X receptors (LXRs), thereby modulating metabolic and physiological functions. Nutritional interventions, feed restriction, and supplementation produce tissue-specific molecular responses in the liver, adipose tissue, mammary gland, and immune system, demonstrating interaction between diet, physiological state, and metabolic regulation. Despite these advances, challenges with genetic and physiological variability, tissue-specific responses, integration of multi-omics data, and translation of molecular findings into practical feeding strategies remain unresolved. Future integration of nutrigenomics with microbiome research, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and precision livestock technologies may facilitate nutritional strategies to improve dairy cattle health, productivity, feed efficiency, and product quality.

title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root.
authors: Denyer, Tom; Solansky, Pavel; Herrmann, Arvid; de Martino, Francesco; Symeonidi, Efthymia; Brosamle, Valentin; Timmermans, Marja C P
abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

title: Varied Ensembles of Long-range ChROmatin interactions drive chromatin compartmentalization.
authors: Ostwal, Yogesh; Muzzopappa, Fernando; Heurteau, Alexandre; Raffel, Raoul; Veluchamy, Alaguraj; Eswara, Karthik; Boudellioua, Ahlem; Ali, Shakila; Kumari, Reema; Depierre, David; Vadlamani, Satya; Schickele, Naomi; Schaak, Stephane; Erdel, Fabian; Cuvier, Olivier; Fischle, Wolfgang
abstract: The chromatin components that are involved in organizing eukaryotic genomes into active and inactive compartments remain unclear. In analysing viable Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking different chromatin-regulatory proteins, we found that the HP1-type factor HPL-2 and the MBT-domain protein LIN-61 jointly contribute to chromatin compartmentalization. Genomic regions bound by both proteins and their cognate histone mark H3 lysine 9 dimethylation (H3K9me2) form broad interfaces of 30-50 kilobases that engage in combinatorial interactions, which we term 'Varied Ensembles of Long-range ChROmatin interactions' (VELCROs). Remarkably, VELCROs are defined by high density of H3K9me2, HPL-2, and LIN-61 sites, but not by the intensity of their individual peaks. Mutants that display defective chromatin compartmentalization are impaired in VELCROs. Polymer simulations show that VELCROs can drive a phase transition that segregates B from A chromatin compartments depending on peak densities. Our work identifies VELCROs as stochastic ensembles of interactions constrained within defined chromatin hubs that shape genome compartmentalization.

title: AI and computational methods for reconstructing cell-state-specific gene regulatory networks from single-cell transcriptome and chromatin accessibility data in cancer: methods, applications, and perspectives.
authors: Wang, Jinying; Chen, Fenjuan
abstract: Tumor heterogeneity is shaped by genetic, epigenetic, microenvironmental, and stochastic factors, among which cell-state-specific regulatory programs are a major determinant. Gene regulatory networks provide a systems-level model linking transcription factors, cis-regulatory elements, and target genes. Paired single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq) measure chromatin accessibility and gene expression in the same cell, offering a direct view of regulatory elements and transcriptional output; matched-but-unpaired, imputed, and single-modality designs can extend coverage but introduce additional assumptions and artifacts. This mini-review focuses on AI and computational methods for reconstructing cell-state-specific GRNs from single-cell transcriptome and chromatin accessibility data in cancer. We define inclusion criteria, distinguish same-cell paired, matched-unpaired, imputed, and single-modality designs, and organize methods by inference objective and input requirement. We cover motif/co-accessibility inference, deep integration and graph learning, dynamic and cell-state-specific modeling, and virtual perturbation. We then discuss applications in epithelial-mesenchymal transition, treatment resistance, lineage plasticity, and tumor subtyping, emphasizing an evidence hierarchy from statistical association to directional prediction, in silico perturbation, and experimentally supported causal regulation. Finally, we examine benchmarking, limitations, and translational prospects. These approaches may help convert GRNs from descriptive maps into testable models of tumor regulation, but clinical utility still requires prospective validation.

title: PSHIC reveals allele-specific chromatin organization by phasing-free structural modeling.
authors: Liu, Wei; Wang, Xueying; Zhang, Yuwei; Pan, Guangze; Li, Shuaicheng
abstract: Resolving the distinct 3D chromatin architectures of parental chromosomes is critical for understanding diploid genome function, but many haplotype-resolved Hi-C contact-map methods remain constrained by their reliance on phased single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). This dependency treats reconstruction as a simple tag-and-sort problem, leading to massive data loss, extreme fragility to phasing errors, and inapplicability in SNP-sparse contexts. We introduce PSHIC, a computational framework that reveals this hidden chromatin organization by employing phasing-free structural modeling, directly from aggregated Hi-C data. PSHIC models chromosomes as continuous manifolds and solves the inverse problem of finding two homolog-specific structures whose combined contacts best explain the observed data. Comprehensive simulations across varying sequencing depths, SNP densities, and phasing error rates demonstrate that PSHIC consistently outperforms established methods, achieving superior accuracy (SCC >/= 0.987), loop detection (F(1)>/= 0.952), and structural fidelity (DER </= 0.04). Applications to real human and mouse Hi-C datasets show that PSHIC recovers known allele-associated features in X-chromosome inactivation, genomic imprinting, and regulatory networks. Results align with orthogonal experimental approaches including 3D DNA-FISH, 4C-seq, and ChIA-PET. PSHIC democratizes diploid chromatin analysis by enabling robust reconstruction in non-model organisms and other SNP-limited or poorly phased contexts.

title: Super-enhancers: regulatory mechanisms, biological functions, diseases, and therapeutic targets.
authors: Miao, Huijie; Liu, Yuanding; Yang, Kaini; Gu, Ao; Zhang, Cuifeng; Li, Mengyao; Wang, Jie
abstract: Super-enhancers (SEs) are operationally defined as clusters of cis-regulatory elements associated with high transcriptional activity and cell-identity genes. They display dense transcription factor and coactivator occupancy, strong H3K27 acetylation, and enhancer-promoter communication, but their annotation varies across platforms, algorithms, and thresholds. This review examines SE architecture, identification, and validation, distinguishing chromatin-based annotation from functional dependence demonstrated by locus-specific perturbations. Mechanisms of SE-associated transcription include pioneer factors, chromatin remodelers, three-dimensional genome organization, transcriptional condensates, non-coding RNAs, and extrachromosomal DNA. Physiological functions in development, immunity, and metabolic homeostasis are considered alongside context-dependent dysregulation in cancer, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and metabolic diseases. Breast cancer provides a model for examining subtype-specific regulation and transcriptional plasticity. Particular attention is given to enhancer remodeling during endocrine therapy, cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibition, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted treatment, and chemotherapy, which may support bypass signaling, stemness, and persistent resistance. Causal regulatory changes must nevertheless be distinguished from correlates of treatment selection. Therapeutic approaches targeting bromodomain and extraterminal domain (BET) proteins, CDK7/9, chromatin regulators, enhancer RNAs, and regulatory loci are critically evaluated. Definitional uncertainty, model dependence, limited reproducibility, systemic toxicity, and insufficient clinical validation remain major barriers. Priorities include standardized annotation, temporally resolved perturbation, single-cell and spatial profiling, artificial intelligence-assisted integration, patient-derived models, and biomarker-guided therapeutic development. Together, these perspectives position SEs as a context-dependent framework linking regulatory architecture to disease progression and treatment resistance, while emphasizing the evidence required to establish therapeutic vulnerabilities.

title: HiCP2GAN: a plug and play foundation model-based GAN for Hi-C enhancement.
authors: Olowofila, Samuel; Oluwadare, Oluwatosin
abstract: The 3D organization of chromatin shapes gene regulation and cellular function, and Hi-C has become the primary technique for mapping chromatin interactions genome-wide. However, high-resolution data remain costly and scarce, leaving many studies with sparse contact maps that limit downstream analysis. Deep learning methods, especially generative adversarial networks (GANs), have shown promise for enhancing low-resolution Hi-C data, but most existing GAN-based approaches rely on custom discriminators trained from scratch, which can yield unstable training and limited generalization. Hi-C foundation models pretrained on large-scale data capture rich, transferable representations of chromatin structure, yet their use as discriminators within adversarial enhancement frameworks had not been explored. We introduce HiCP2GAN, a plug-and-play GAN that employs a pretrained Vision Transformer-based Hi-C foundation model as its discriminator. The discriminator was pretrained on 118 million Hi-C patches across diverse species and cell types, providing biologically meaningful gradients for adversarial supervision. The framework is generator-agnostic: any compatible Hi-C resolution enhancement architecture can serve as the generator, enabling fair comparison across methods. The encoder phase of the foundation model was adapted as a discriminator backbone, finetuning the first few layers from the input while freezing the deeper transformer layers to preserve pretrained knowledge while allowing task-specific adaptation. Experiments across various cell lines show that HiCP2GAN outperforms traditional GAN-based methods in most settings and improves the reconstruction quality and biological reproducibility of existing Hi-C enhancement models in most evaluated cases. HiCP2GAN is publicly available at https://github.com/OluwadareLab/HiCP2GAN.

title: AxialTAD: an axial contrast architecture for TAD boundary prediction from Hi-C.
authors: Choi, Woo-Young; Rhee, Je-Keun
abstract: Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of 3D chromatin organization, and accurate identification of TAD boundaries from Hi-C contact matrices remains an active challenge. Recent deep learning approaches have advanced substantially, but these rely on increasingly large architectures, raising the question of how much of this capacity boundary-centric analysis requires. Here we propose AxialTAD, a compact deep learning model centered on an Axial Contrast Module (ACM) that explicitly encodes directional contrast in contact intensity along the row and column axes of local Hi-C patches, an operator aligned with the geometric signature of TAD boundaries. Evaluated on four human cell lines (GM12878, HeLa-S3, IMR-90, K562) within cell lines and under leave-one-cell-out generalization, AxialTAD performed comparably with a recent convolutional neural network (CNN)+Transformer baseline (deepTAD) while using 76%-80% fewer trainable parameters (113K-137K versus 571K). A parameter-matched conventional CNN achieved similar F1 to AxialTAD in the human 25 kb experiments. When trained and evaluated within each of two mouse datasets, AxialTAD outperformed both this control and deepTAD. Orthogonal validation against CTCF and cohesin ChIP-seq supported the biological plausibility of the predicted boundaries. These results indicate that, within the range of architectures examined, a large architecture is not necessary to reach this level of boundary prediction.

title: Multi-task adversarial autoencoder for functional genomic element generation with preserved biophysical properties.
authors: Adamu, Shamsuddeen; Alhussian, Hitham; Abdulkadir, Said Jadid; Eltahir, Majdy Mohamed Eltayeb; Khairy, Sallam O F; Hassan, Ibrahim Hayatu; Kurah, Ibrahim Muhammad; Mukhtar, Abubakar; Ganesalingam, Vijayakanthan; Ravi, Vaishali; Saidu, Yahaya
abstract: Generative modeling of genomic sequences presents a stringent test for deep learning, requiring the capture of long-range dependencies and functional constraints beyond local nucleotide statistics. Existing architectures frequently collapse to limited modes or reproduce shallow nucleotide distributions without encoding functional semantics. We introduce the Multi-Task Adversarial Autoencoder (MT-AAE), a hybrid generative framework that integrates adversarial regularization with auxiliary functional and biophysical objectives to enforce structured latent representations. Evaluated on an empirical human gene corpus, MT-AAE achieved a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TRTS) accuracy of 74.7%, compared with 41.0% for a standard GAN baseline. Stratified analysis further showed that functional discriminability increased to 89.3% when sequence lengths aligned with the model's architectural window. Importantly, the learned representations exhibited emergent biological structure: synthetic sequences spontaneously preserved cis-regulatory syntax, including canonical TATA-box motifs recovered across 100% of generated promoter sequences without explicit rule encoding, though positional placement relative to the TSS was not statistically significant (KS [Formula: see text]), and the high occurrence rate is partly attributable to the AT-rich composition of the generated sequences. Representation-level validation using frozen DNABERT-2 and DNABERT-S embeddings confirmed that the generated sequences retained functional information beyond shallow k-mer statistics. Cross-species evaluation on Mus musculus sequences further demonstrated species-specific learning consistent with known human-mouse regulatory divergence. The framework also mitigated mode collapse, maintaining near-uniform generation across functional classes ([Formula: see text]), including rare categories such as tRNAs ([Formula: see text] of the dataset). These findings position MT-AAE as an effective framework for biologically constrained genomic sequence generation.

title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
authors: Peng Y; Yang L; Ge H
abstract:
Motivation

Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell’s own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing.

Results

We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles.

Availability

scSTEC is freely available at https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC .

title: Gene Embedding Hub: a standardized resource for human gene representations
authors: Tabares D; Bohl M; Boeva V
abstract: Gene embeddings are vector representations of gene identity that provide machine-learning models with information from diverse biological sources. However, their use is hindered by a lack of standardization: inconsistent identifiers, formats, and preprocessing conventions. In this work, we present a unified resource of 67 human gene-embedding sets derived from protein, DNA and RNA sequences, biomedical text, bulk expression data, single-cell expression models, functional data, biological networks, knowledge graphs, regulatory genomics and multimodal models, covering up to 20,097 GENCODE-annotated protein-coding genes. The collection includes both published precomputed embeddings and representations generated or extracted from publicly available models and biological data. Each embedding set is organized in a folder containing the embedding matrix, the Ensembl gene identifiers, machine-readable metadata, and processing documentation. We validate the resource by measuring global and local similarity, cross-embedding consensus, and cross-embedding predictability. The collection is designed to allow community-contributed embeddings that meet predefined technical and documentation requirements, enables comparison of gene representations across modalities and provides standardized embeddings for training and downstream applications.

title: A compact motif vocabulary is differentially interpreted across human cell types
authors: Shen S; Wang W
abstract: How a common genome generates diverse human cell types may depend less on distinct cis-regulatory vocabularies than on context-dependent use of a shared one. We have developed CNN-CR, an interpretable neural network that learns regulatory motifs while predicting gene expression across 116 human biosamples. Promoter regulation proves highly compressible: dozens of recurrent motif families retain most of the predictive information of much larger cell-type-specific vocabularies and generalize to cellular contexts excluded from their discovery. These motifs are conserved at their binding sites and enriched at fine-mapped regulatory variants. Cellular context acts at two levels: chromatin state gates which motif instances are available for regulatory use, whereas reader identity determines how accessible motifs are interpreted. ChIP-seq data reveal frequent shifts in reader occupancy across cell types, and genome-scale perturbations support corresponding context-dependent reader functions. Thus, regulatory diversity can emerge through differential access to and interpretation of a compact shared DNA vocabulary.

title: A single-cell multimodal foundation model enables cross modality analysis between transcriptome and chromatin
authors: Bao X; Zhu J; Song X; Zhang X; Zeng H; Vu HT; Zhang H; Zhang Z; Yao M; Liang M; Liu K; Parker SC; Chen S; Liu J
abstract: Most single-cell studies measure either gene expression or chromatin accessibility, and connecting the two usually requires fitting a model to each study. Here we present MUTUAL (MUltiome Transfer in a Unified Aligned Latent space), which keeps the single-cell foundation models scFoundation and EpiAgent frozen, combines their embeddings with linear summaries of each modality and learns a shared RNA– ATAC space from 3.0 million paired cells of 400 public multiome datasets. Applied without refitting to ten datasets not used for training, MUTUAL matched cells’ RNA and ATAC profiles more accurately than methods fitted on other donors of the same dataset, annotated ATAC-only cells more accurately and transferred transcription-factor motif activity to RNA-only cells beyond what cell-type assignment provides. In a maturation series of stem-cell-derived islets, motif activity predicted from RNA largely reproduced the measured stage-wise changes when other libraries of the series served as the reference. MUTUAL makes public multiome data directly usable by single-modality studies.

title: MUSS: A Multi-scale and Sequence-based Model for Single-cell Gene Regulation
authors: Kangjie Zheng; Amirhossein Vahidi; Liying Jin; Joseph Clarke; Vijaya Baskar MS; Connor Rogerson; Mengji Zhang; Muzlifah Haniffa; Anshul Kundaje; Mo Lotfollahi
abstract: Modeling gene regulation in single cells requires jointly representing DNA sequence, chromatin accessibility, and gene expression across regulatory scales. Sequence-based models capture DNA-level regulatory grammar but often lack cell-level resolution, whereas many single-cell omics models represent genes and peaks as fixed-vocabulary tokens without their underlying sequence. Here, we present MUSS, a sequence-based multi-scale model for single-cell gene regulation that preserves both DNA-level and cell-level resolution. MUSS derives peak- and gene-level representations from DNA using a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder and integrates them through peak-peak self-attention and distance-biased peak-gene interactions. Peak masked language modeling followed by training on paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq aligns these representations with cell-specific regulatory states. Across gene expression prediction, enhancer-gene linking, motif-guided regulatory prioritization, and zero-shot cell clustering, MUSS achieves strong performance against sequence-based and single-cell omics baselines. It further predicts expression for genes and peaks unseen during task training. These results support sequence-grounded, multi-scale representations for decoding cell-type-specific regulatory programs. Code, datasets, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/MUSS_neurips26.

title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
authors: Arda Uzunoglu; Mahler Revsine; Michael Schatz; Benjamin Van Durme; Mehrdad Farajtabar; Daniel Khashabi; Eric Nalisnick
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.
